payload.native_system_prompt:
You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

### Glossary of tags that will be sent to you:
# - <LM_SYSTEM_PROMPT>: The system prompt for the language model.
# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Change the background into a basketball court
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: Is the visible background recognizably a basketball court?
node.criteria: pass: visible court features make the background recognizably a basketball court. fail: the visible background is clearly not a basketball court. unknown: the background is not sufficiently visible or clear to decide.
node.binding: The image background and whether it depicts a basketball court.

node_traces.evidence: The edited image shows a basketball hoop and net, basketballs, and court markings on the floor, making the background recognizably a basketball court.

The edited background shows a basketball hoop, balls, and court markings, but no recognizable basketball-court setting; it is predominantly a plain dark backdrop. The visible background therefore does not meet the criterion for being recognizably a basketball court.

The edited background shows a basketball hoop, balls, and court markings, but the visible setting is not recognizably a basketball court; it appears to be a dark, featureless backdrop with a strip of court-like floor. The proposition that the background is recognizably a basketball court is therefore not met.
The edited background visibly includes a basketball hoop, basketballs, and court markings, making it recognizably a basketball court. The source background was a kitchen.
The edited background visibly depicts a basketball court, with a hoop and net, court floor, and painted court lines. The source background is a kitchen.

n3: The binding is malformed and underspecified: “with the (...)” leaves the visual criterion open, and the node’s yes/no question does not itself distinguish a completed background replacement from partial progress. Tighten the typed criterion so completion depends on whether the background as a whole is recognizably a basketball-court setting, while treating isolated basketball props or court-like markings as progress only when the saved evidence supports that distinction. The edited image shows a hoop, balls, and a marked floor, but most of the setting is a plain dark backdrop; this is genuine visual ambiguity about completion, not a transport or dependency failure. Preserve the existing complete/partial/absent/unknown mapping and use the saved n1/n2 evidence consistently: n1’s recognizability judgment determines completion, while n2 can establish specific progress when n1 fails. The traces alternate between complete and partial despite nearly identical evidence, often treating the same props as sufficient to make the setting recognizable. Clarify that inference boundary and require evidence to address the overall setting, not merely list court-related objects. Do not force the reference “yes,” equate high confidence or repeated agreement with correctness, or turn uncertainty into a negative; investigate why the recognizability assessment varies.
